claims.content: Stevie's absence on his villegiature with Michaelis has allowed Mrs Verloc to be alone more often in both shop and house, which becomes significant when Mr Verloc goes out early for the bomb outrage and returns shaken.

Mr Verloc was present at Greenwich Park during the bombing but did not fire the bomb himself — he heard it too soon after arriving, started running, and saw no one until past George Street, though two men were seen entering together.
The overcoat found with Stevie's address sewn inside in marking ink is evidence that either Stebie or someone connected to him committed theft near Michaelis's country cottage.

Mrs Verloc genuinely knows nothing of the bomb affair — she has not read newspapers, and her husband has never told her anything directly; her ignorance appears genuine rather than feigned even when Heat presses her.

Mr Verloc plans to make a full confession about what he did in Greenwich Park and expects that this will 'upset many things' despite his own reputation as a straight man who kept straight for those people too long.

claims.content: Most criminals feel an irresistible need to confess — of making a clean breast of it to somebody, often to the police. Verloc was in this state: he flung himself on the Assistant Commissioner's breast upon hearing 'I know that you are at the bottom of this affair.'
The victim blown up in Greenwich Park is Stevie (Winnie's brother-in-law), and Mr Verloc did not plan his death but was shocked by it.

Michaelis, the ex-convict who took Stevie temporarily into his country lodgings, has nothing to do with the explosion — he could have no suspicion of anything unusual since Verloc regularly took the boy out for walks on such occasions.
The affair is a domestic drama: Verloc's wife would not go abroad and Stevie was genuine brother-in-law from a certain point of view.

English police have cleared the identity of the victim in less than twelve hours — establishing who was blown to shreds, finding the organiser (Verloc), glimpsing the inciter behind him (Mr Vladimir).
Foreign political spies and agents provocateurs are a 'ghastly nuisance' and an element of danger; the way is to make their employment unpleasant to their employers.

claims.content: Mrs Verloc is guilty of murder — she struck Mr Verloc down herself — yet the only murderer people will find in the room when they come looking is herself.
The stab that killed Mr Verloc was an obscurely prompted blow, but the blood trickling from the knife handle transforms it into a plain case of murder for any court to see.
Mrs Verloc's terror is not of death itself — she tried and failed at suicide long before — but of being hanged with the fourteen-foot drop in the quiet presence of authorities inside jail walls.

Mr Verloc, though he seemed kind and good-natured throughout their seven-year marriage, was a devil who stole Stevie from his mother by sending him to die in Greenwich Park under the pretence of a humanitarian enterprise.
Ossipon's love for Mrs Verloc — or at least his belief that she loves him back — is real enough as instinctive self-preservation acts upon a drowning woman grasping at any messenger of life.

claims.content: Madness and despair are not genuine conditions but forces that exist only insofar as they threaten mediocrity; Verloc was mediocre and the police murdered him because he lacked force.
The weak — flabby, cowardly, slavish of mind — rule the earth through their sheer multitude, and their power is so total that even death serves them.
Science will eventually serve only the strong; doctors who cure rather than kill are advancing toward a world where science reigns in the shade but rules at last.
Mankind does not know what it wants, though the Professor himself knows — he needs time to complete his great work of extermination before the multitude crushes him.
